brief.ask: Create a brand identity for Emberwick, the coffee roaster whose website is in this folder.
brief.owner: Owner preferences: warm, crafted and quietly confident, not rustic or hipster; for people who care where their coffee comes from. No coffee beans, cups, steam, mountains or flames drawn literally. Web shop, bag labels and stickers, social, and a mark that works stamped in one colour.

claim.notes: Seven directions over two rounds (4 developed and verified with 0 measured fails) all failed or were dropped at the critic's quality gate (best: impression, blind avg 6.2, read as §), so nothing was finalized or exported.

concepts.title: Crossed w
concepts.sketchNotes: Reads as: s1 a W monogram with a diamond hole (sporty/automotive badge); s2 'Wi' with a diamond tittle, the round-1 dot-on-i trick again; s3 a W with a tall pointed middle, still a W; s4 an app-icon tile with a W, UI geometry; s5 two offset Vs, a stepped copy of the initial. All five are the name's initial with an overlap/cut/offset device, and the sharp sheared angles read corporate-sporty, not warm or crafted. The 'ember' hole reads as a plain rhombus. Do not develop; drop the W-monogram route rather than rework it.

concepts.title: Direct line
concepts.sketchNotes: Reads as: s1 an awareness ribbon (or a lasso / pin), with a ball on the end; s2 a striped bug or bee, or a ball of yarn (an insect is a bad reading for a food brand); s3 a spiral in a disc, a snail shell or a 9/6 in a circle, stock shape 77%. All struck: cliché ribbon, unfortunate insect, stock spiral. A looped thread does not say 'direct relationship with eight farms' to a stranger. Different move: drop the thread-loop. If traceability stays the idea, express it as one straight, unbroken line from origin to bag that ends in a specific mark (e.g. a single rule with eight ticks/impressions behind a solid stop, built like a printer's rule), or merge the idea into the stamp/roast-date label system rather than the symbol.

concepts.title: Eight
concepts.sketchNotes: Reads as: s1 a dotted selection/crop frame, UI; s2 a keypad or tile grid, pattern not mark; s3 a cluster of drop/petal shapes like a dice face or ornament, the most mark-like; s4 a loading spinner, struck. Keep s3: a 3-2-3 rhythm that stamps well and has its own silhouette. Risks: reads as dice/braille or generic dot pattern, and the half-round drops edge toward beans or petals; nobody will count eight farms. In development: give the eight units one decisive printer's-ornament shape (a fleuron or quad-like sort) so the cluster reads as set type, tighten spacing so the whole reads as one lozenge at 16 px rather than eight dots, and avoid any bean/drop reading.

concepts.title: Ember dot
readsAs: a lowercase serif i with a chunky tilted dot
a coal or rock on a stem (unfortunate: the help/info button)
concepts.sketchNotes: Reads as: s1 a serif i with a red dot (the 'i' info icon; colour-dot-over-i is a stock wordmark trick); s2 a heavy e with a red spot in its eye, the spot is lost at 16 px; s3 a k with a red blob stuck in its crook, arbitrary; s4 a slant-topped i with a coal sitting just off the cut, the only one where the dot has a reason (trimmed wick); s5 a slab 1 under a red life-ring/donut. Struck s1, s5 (info icon / numeral 1 plus ring). Keep s4: the slanted wick cut and the coal. Main risk: a standalone i still reads as the info glyph, so develop it inside the Emberwick wordmark (Fraunces-like serif, the wick i carries the coal) and use the cut stem plus coal as the icon only after it is ownable there. Make the coal a deliberate, single-colour-stampable shape (not a random pebble), tie its angle to the cut, keep no hairlines, and check that the coal does not read as a flame or a blood drop.

concepts.title: Impression
readsAs: a lowercase e stacked on an upside-down e
concepts.sketchNotes: Reads as: s1 an 'e' stacked on a '6', then a symmetric ornamental glyph like a section sign; s2 'e6' on a keycap/slab; s3 'e9' with a UI tile; s4 an e over a 6 merging into a figure-eight. Keep s1: warm heavy serif e, one solid shape, on-brief printworks idea, stamps cleanly with no hairlines, unlike anything at Square Mile/Origin/Workshop. Main risk is the 'e6' (chess move / number) reading. In development: make it read as one glyph, not two characters: true point symmetry with a shared joining bar or ink bridge, lower half clearly the pressed print (e.g. heavier, inked-in counter or slightly spread as an impression), and kill the 6-like tail of the lower terminal. Test against &, § and 8 at 16 px.

concepts.title: The sort
readsAs: a rubber stamp with an e on it
a perfume bottle or kitchen weight
an approve/stamp UI icon (unfortunate: office paperwork tool)
concepts.sketchNotes: Reads as: s1 an e on a book/app tile (bottom groove reads as page edges); s2 an e in a bracket frame, a UI/app glyph, weak at 16 px; s3 an e on a podium or shelf; s4 a rubber hand stamp with an e on its face (second reading: a perfume bottle or jar); s5 an e tile with its bar run out of the edge (initial with a cut). Struck s1, s2 (initial in a box), s5 (cut monogram), s3 (podium). Keep s4: it is the only one that draws the brand's own differentiator, the printworks stamp that marks the bags. Risks: an initial-in-a-shape is generic, and the knob-and-neck silhouette drifts to bottle/jar. In development, make the stamp body unmistakable (proportion of handle to base, maybe the face shown mid-impression or the e mirrored like a real stamp face) and give the e a custom, ownable cut, not a stock serif. Must survive one-colour rubber stamping.

concepts.title: Warm house
concepts.sketchNotes: Reads as: s1 a fireplace or bread/pizza oven with a glow (also a gravestone or mouse hole); s2 a keyhole or a figure/candle under an arch; s3 an oven or fireplace on a shelf; s4 the letters n and l, or a bar chart. All struck: the glowing arch reads as an oven/fireplace, a back door to the banned flames, and the arched doorway is the most worn café/bakery trope of the decade; s4 reads as letters/bars. Different move: if 'welcome' matters, get it from the printworks, not a doorway; e.g. the shop's warmth as a lit window drawn as a printed block/impression, or abandon the house idea and fold warmth into colour and type.
